Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What was the most legendary thing your grandmother did?
Answer: My Gramma, Catherine “Kitty” Finnegan, was her parents' oldest surviving child — they had 8 kids, but four, including their firstborn, Annie, died in childhood. My great-grandmother, Mary, had her 8th child, my great-uncle Joe, in March of 1922. Gramma was 13, her brother John was 7, and her sister Elizabeth (Lee) was three and a half. Mary died of childbirth complications shortly after Joe's birth, leaving her husband John a single father of four, including a newborn. My great-grandfather was not a wealthy man. He also had no family in the United States; they were all back in Ireland, as he and Mary had immigrated in 1907. So he was faced with the very real possibility of having to put his children in an orphanage, because he could not afford a nanny and had to work. But the kids didn't end up in an orphanage. Because Gramma raised her three younger siblings herself. 13 years old, and she took on a 7-year-old, a toddler, and a newborn. She did the cooking and cleaning and washing, she got them fed and off to school. It must have been incredibly difficult, and in her later years, my Gramma wore her early life's hardship all over her face, which always looked older than its years. She was also an eternally patient woman, and I guess she'd have to have learned patience, basically being the mother to three kids when she was mostly still a kid herself. But she kept her family together. I remember myself at 13, and there is literally no way I could have raised three kids. I couldn't have raised one kid. I've always seen my Gramma — who also, as an adult, went on to raise four kids of her own, and to handle all the family's bills and finances, since my Grampa was illiterate — as possibly the most badass woman ever. That's my Gramma on the right, with my Great-Uncle Mike (Lee's husband), my Grampa Jack, my Uncle Jackie, and my mom. Taken at my grandparents' apartment in the Bronx in the mid-1950s.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Is Stephen Stills a good musician?
Answer: Of course he is. From a technical standpoint, he's a great musician, even. Crosby, Stills and Nash's legendary first album was largely Stephen's creation; he had an artistic vision, and David Crosby and Graham Nash let him run with it. Other than the drums (which were played by Dallas Taylor), Stills played every instrument on that album, which is how he got the nickname Captain Manyhands. His double album with Manassas is pretty epic, too, and he wrote just about everything on it. He also hasn't limited himself to one genre, or even a couple of them. Folk, rock, Latin, blues, jazz, country, Stephen has at least dabbled in all of them. He can produce sounds on a single acoustic guitar that most people can't even imagine. Brilliant guitarist. If anything has hindered him throughout the years, it's been his personality. He was said to be a type-A, control freak kind of guy, especially creatively, which is why he butted heads so often with his friend Neil Young, who is reportedly fairly similar. He also reputedly really liked that nasty cocaine in his youth, which probably only amplified the negative aspects of his personality. But I do hear he has mellowed quite a bit with age (and sobriety). Anyway, yes — Stephen Stills is a very good musician.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Is The Breakfast Club still relevant?
Answer: It's been a long time since I was a teenager, but… Do teens still feel peer pressure from their friends? Do they still feel pressure from their families to succeed, be it at academics, athletics, etc.? Do they still feel misunderstood or ignored by their parents? Do they still feel like their teachers and other authority figures judge them harshly without knowing their individual struggles? Do they still judge kids from other cliques without knowing them? Do they still feel alone and alienated if they don't fit in? If the answer to any or all of these is “yes" then… yeah, The Breakfast Club is still relevant. The whole point of the movie is that teenagers often struggle to feel understood by the adults in their lives, and also are often pressured by their friends and peer groups. Also that once you get past the superficial differences, many teenagers have similar feelings, and feel similar pressures (like Brian with his grades and Andy with his wrestling), and that if kids in different cliques would just take the time to talk — and listen — to one another, they might not feel so different from each other. My experience is that these are things that happen across generations. They weren't specific to Gen X; the film just happened to be made when Gen X were teenagers.

Question: What is the most obscure reference you noticed in a movie or television show?
Answer: In The Rock, Sean Connery plays former SAS agent John Mason, who escaped Alcatraz in 1962. When Nicolas Cage's character introduces himself to Mason, saying, “I'm Stanley Goodspeed", Mason responds dryly, “of course you are". This is the same reply Connery, as James Bond, gives to Lana Wood's character Plenty O'Toole in Diamonds Are Forever when he meets her in the casino and she says, “hi, I'm Plenty”. Question: Why do Americans always equate England to London. Do you not know we have other large cities?
Answer: As if the average Englishman could name any major U.S. cities other than New York City, Los Angeles, and maybe San Francisco or Chicago. Philadelphia has a larger population than any English city other than London, and most Brits who've even heard of it probably only know it because it's the title of a Tom Hanks movie. Houston, Phoenix, San Antonio, Dallas, and San Diego are also bigger than any city in England aside from London, and San Jose, Austin, and Jacksonville are not far behind. There are nine cities in the U.S. with populations greater than one million (and that's the city proper, not the metro area), and ten more with populations between 700,000 and one million. Yet I'd wager that a majority of English people couldn't name more than 4 or 5 of them at most. Many, maybe even most, Americans have heard of cities like Manchester, Liverpool, and Birmingham. I personally also know cities like Sheffield, Cambridge, Milton Keynes, and Nottingham. (For the record, Nottingham’s population is roughly the same as that of Stockton, California, which even a fair number of Americans have never heard of.) But when almost one fifth of your country's entire population lives in the greater London area, and most of the movies and media we see set in England are set in or around London, what do you expect? Cut us some slack, man. I don't care if you've heard of Indianapolis or Louisville or Albuquerque. EDIT: Folks, being able to name Stamford, Connecticut or Durham, North Carolina because they're named after English cities doesn't make you well-informed about American city names. Connecticut has a ton of cities and towns named after places in England, and kids who grow up in Danbury and surrounding areas are well aware that there's a Danbury in England that the city is named after.

Question: Is there an action movie that examines philosophical issues?
Answer: Runaway Train, that overlooked gem of 80s action films. Directed by Andrei Konchalovsky, with a screenplay by Eddie Bunker and Paul Zindel, and a story by Akira Kurosawa (who initially planned to direct in 1966, but couldn't get studio backing in the U.S. and so abandoned the project), it stars Jon Voight and Eric Roberts, both of whom received Oscar nominations for their performances. Voight — a hulking powerhouse here — is Oscar “Manny" Manheim, a vicious bank robber and hardened career criminal, who was welded into his tiny cell in Alaska's Stonehaven Prison after two escapes. Those escapes, and his three years in solitary, have made him a hero to his fellow inmates, none more so than Buck McGeehy (Roberts), a dumb, naive young prizefighter in for statutory rape. After a court order deems Manny's confinement unconstitutional and he is returned to general population, the brutal warden, Ranken (John P. Ryan), attempts to have him shanked, leading Manny to plot another escape in the dead of the Alaskan winter. He enlists Buck, a laundry trusty, to help, and the starstruck youngster convinces Manny to take him along. Buck and Manny hop a train consisting only of four locomotives, intending to ride to freedom, but unbeknownst to them, the engineer suffers a heart attack and falls from the train, leaving it speeding through the wilderness at higher and higher speeds. They eventually learn that there's one other person on board, locomotive hostler Sara (Rebecca DeMornay), but she, too, is powerless to stop the train, whose emergency stop is located on the inaccessible first engine. While the action sequences are dynamite, it's also on the train that the film waxes most philosophical. Manny is institutionalized; even if he earned a legal parole, he wouldn't know how to live a normal life. He's beyond redemption. Buck is not so far gone, but he romanticizes both Manny and the criminal lifestyle, testing Manny's patience. Manny envies Buck, in a sense, because Buck still has a chance, still has most of his humanity, something Manny jettisoned a long time ago, and Buck's seeming determination to ruin his life beyond repair frustrates Manny. However, at the same time, Manny's viciousness becomes only too evident in this desperate situation, and the film asks the question, is Manny an animal? Or is he only too human? I won't get into further detail about the plot, or the epic ending, but I'll leave you with the same Shakespeare quote (from Richard III) as the film does: No beast so fierce but knows some touch of pity. But I know none, and therefore am no beast.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Do Certain animals have more rights than others?
Answer: In Western human society? Of course. Our “favorite" animals, namely dogs and cats, are often put on a pedestal, and injustice done to a dog or cat is seen as a horrific thing. But the mistreatment of other domestic animals doesn't evoke the same level of indignation and outrage for some reason. Horses, for example, are mistreated all the time, often under the guise of “training”. There are still people who use the term “breaking” a horse, which literally means breaking its spirit. If a horse is mistreated and lashes out, it's often deemed “dangerous” and put down. People still put metal bits in horses' mouths, which causes great pain, even though there are bitless bridles readily available these days. Horse racing is inherently animal abuse; racehorses die all the time, and most of them are also given PEDs. Tennessee Walking Horses are sored, with caustic chemicals applied to their legs to enhance their gait. Saddlebreds are also sored and forced to wear heavy shoes and chains on their feet. (Soring is illegal in the U.S., for the record, but people still do it and unethical vets are paid to sign off on the horse's health.) Carriage horses in major cities like New York live horrible lives. They never get to run in a pasture or just be horses; they're either on the streets pulling dumb tourists around or they're locked in a stall. When they collapse from exhaustion, they're whipped and beaten. (For the record, horses have thinner skin and more nerve endings than humans do, meaning it's more painful for them to be whipped than it is for us.) These aren't animals to their owners, they're machines and commodities, that exist only to make their owners money, and they get nothing whatsoever in return for it. People also routinely ride horses that are not big enough to safely carry them; I've seen videos of people weighing over 200 pounds riding miniature horses that probably weigh less than they do, when the general rule is that a rider should weigh no more than 15 to 20% of the horse's body weight (and 20% is pushing it). That means if you're 200 pounds, you shouldn't be riding any horse less than 1,100 pounds (most saddle horses are between 800 and 1,100 pounds). Many horse riding facilities have weight limits in place for riders, usually around 220 pounds. There was an incident awhile back where a plus-sized TikTok model, whom I think weighed around 250 pounds, raised a stink because a horse riding facility on Long Island wouldn't allow her to ride, because they didn't have any horses big enough to safely carry her. She called them fatphobic and discriminatory. For not letting her abuse an animal. (One of the employees at the stable did later fat shame her in a TikTok, which was 100% wrong, and I believe he was fired over it, but that doesn't change the fact that this girl thought it was somehow her right to ride a horse, even if it could injure the animal. It's not about being fat, it's strictly about weight. A 5′9″, 150lb person is not likely to be overweight, but they're still too heavy to ride a 500lb Welsh pony, just as a 250lb person is too heavy to ride a 1,000lb Quarter Horse or Morgan. By the same token, a 5′0″, 160lb person IS overweight, but can still ride a 1,000lb horse.) Other animals are also abused and mistreated all the time, often just for clicks and views on TikTok or Instagram. Fish are routinely abused on TikTok. Rabbits are abused on TikTok. Hamsters are abused on TikTok. Birds are abused on TikTok. Reptiles are abused on TikTok. Horses are abused on TikTok. And these videos often have millions of likes and views. We're talking blatant animal abuse, and nobody cares. People think it's funny to see a rabbit thrown into a swimming pool and forced to swim, even though they can die of shock or hypothermia. It's hilarious to see a plus sized person riding a 200lb mini horse that's in pain, panting, and wheezing from the weight on its back. Watching goldfish gasp for breath out of water, or hamsters forced to run Squid Game-like obstacle courses? OMG, sooo funny! Do some animals have more rights than others? You bet your ass they do, and it's wrong on so many levels.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What actor/actress’ film career came undone due to blacklisting?
Answer: Anne Revere. I just mentioned her in another answer, so she's fresh in my mind. A native of New York City (and a direct descendant of Revolutionary War icon Paul Revere), she began her acting career on Broadway in the early 1930s, and then in film in 1934. She became known for playing mothers, and won the Best Supporting Actress Oscar for her fantastic performance as Elizabeth Taylor's mother in National Velvet. She had previously been nominated for playing Jennifer Jones' mother in Song of Bernadette, and was nominated again for playing Gregory Peck's mother in Gentlemen's Agreement (despite being only 13 years older than Peck). With Taylor in National Velvet: Revere was a lifelong Democrat, a self-professed “damn Yankee", and a vocal critic of the McCarthy hearings and the House Un-American Activities Committee. When she was called to testify before the committee in 1950, she invoked her Fifth Amendment rights and refused, leading her to be blacklisted at the height of her career, aged 47. She would not appear in another film until 1970’s Tell Me That You Love Me, Junie Moon, when she was 67. Revere, who was married to theater director Samuel Rosen for nearly 50 years until his death in 1984 (although the couple had no children, perhaps somewhat ironically given her history of playing mothers), died in 1990 at age 87, with only three acting credits on her resume since 1951. One of film's best, most reliable, and most popular actors simply disappeared overnight.

Question: Why was Henry Thomas replaced with Timothy Hutton as (elder Hugh Crain) in the "Haunting of Hill House"?
Answer: Because 99% of the time, old age makeup looks fake as hell, and it can impede an actor's performance. The events in the “past" sequences take place over 20 years prior to the events of the modern sequences. People age in 20 years. If Hugh was supposed to be around 40 when they moved into Hill House — and that seems about right, given the age of the kids — then he's at least 60 in the modern scenes. Henry Thomas, like Carla Gugino, was 46 when the series was filmed, Tim Hutton was 57, but frankly, Thomas was a youthful 46 and Hutton an older-looking 57. My biggest issue is that Thomas has brown eyes and Hutton's are bright blue, so they put blue contacts on Thomas, and blue contacts on dark eyes almost always look unnatural. Flanagan did the old age makeup on Alex Essoe in Midnight Mass, but that I understood even if it was obviously makeup, because she had to gradually de-age from 80 to about 30. That wasn't the case in Hill House. Personally, I thought both Thomas and Hutton were fantastic. As I understand it, they spent time together and Hutton tried to mimic Thomas's mannerisms and speech patterns. But they're both terrific actors, and both did a great job. If they'd put old age makeup on Thomas, it would have been distracting, similar to how the blue contacts were distracting but probably worse. I was actually more struck by seeing Hutton and Annabeth Gish both in the series — they played boyfriend and girlfriend in Beautiful Girls in 1995, and their 11-year age difference is a lot more obvious these days than it was then.

Question: What if my pet is a caged animal? Can a landlord restrict it?
Answer: In the U.S., at least in everyplace I've lived, a landlord can restrict any kind of pets they want. Some landlords will actually allow dogs and/or cats but not allow rabbits; that's how I ended up with my first rabbit — he belonged to my coworker's daughter, and they found out right before moving into a new apartment complex that although it allowed dogs and cats, it didn't allow rabbits. So they asked me to take him rather than bringing him back to the Humane Society. Some people still view rabbits as livestock or outdoor animals, and that can affect their decision to allow or not allow them. I had that same rabbit when I moved from Boulder, Colorado (where my apartment complex had no restrictions on caged animals, just a no dogs policy) to Denver, and I had to pay a non-refundable $300 pet fee to have him. In my current apartment, I had to pay a pet deposit equal to one month's rent for my rabbit and guinea pig. (My rabbit lives in a large pen during the day and overnight, but free roams in my living room every evening.) The bottom line is, you need to ask the landlord, even if it says cats or dogs are allowed. The first thing I asked my current landlord when I called about the apartment was whether rabbits and guinea pigs were allowed, because the listing just said cats. Most landlords probably won't have a problem with a hamster or a couple of gerbils, or even a pair of guinea pigs, but you never know, and some landlords will strictly forbid rabbits even if they allow dogs and cats. And please, do not try to keep any pets if your lease forbids them, no matter how small or quiet they are. If you get caught you could face eviction or, at the very least, having to surrender your pet(s).

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why shouldn't hoarders be allowed to have children or pets?
Answer: Because children and pets shouldn't have to live in spaces like this: They didn't make the decision to hoard out the house, and they shouldn't be forced to live in squalor, under unsafe conditions, because the parent or pet owner has a mental illness. If you can't even properly take care of yourself, you cannot properly take care of children or animals. Kids who grow up in hoarded houses are often ostracized at school, because they tend to smell like the hoarded home — I've seen numerous children of hoarders say this happened to them — and they can't have friends over because of the conditions in the house, so their social development is often stunted. Hoarded houses are also usually extremely unsanitary and hazardous to the health of both humans and animals. In hoarding situations, children and pets are innocent bystanders, at the mercy of the hoarder. It's not fair, it's bad for their physical and mental health, and they shouldn't have to live like that. If you want your kids and pets in your home, get therapy and clean up.

Question: Are there any specific pet breeds that are more likely to develop certain health conditions?
Answer: Rabbit breeds with lop ears and brachycephalic (short) faces are much more likely to develop certain health problems than breeds with normal faces and upright ears. People tend to love lops — the Holland lop, which is also highly brachycephalic, is presently the most popular breed of pet rabbit in both the U.S. and UK — because they look kind of like stuffed animals, but the harsh truth is that lop ears are totally unnatural for rabbits. The shape of the ears means there is a kink in the ear canal, making it narrower and increasing the chances of hearing impairment or even total deafness. Lops are also more prone to earwax buildup, ear infections, and severe mite infestations than erect-eared rabbits. And while it's not necessarily a health problem, per se, communication with other rabbits is more difficult for lops, because they can't move their ears the way they're supposed to be able to. The position of a rabbit's ears tells you a lot about their mood, but the range of motion in lop ears is limited. The shape of a lop's skull also makes them more likely to have dental problems like malocclusion, molar spurs, and overgrown molars, and lop breeds that are also especially brachycephalic — like the Holland lop — may require the extraction of teeth due to misalignment and overgrowth. This also goes for erect-eared breeds that are brachycephalic. Rabbits' teeth have open roots and never stop growing, so their incisors need to line up perfectly in order not to overgrow. A brachycephalic head in rabbits means the lower jaw is longer than the upper jaw, and that can lead the teeth to become misaligned. One recent study indicated that lop rabbits are 15 times more likely to experience significant discomfort during vet examinations, 12 times more likely to experience molar overgrowth, and 23 times more likely to have incisor disease than erect-eared rabbits. Brachycephalic rabbits also are prone to respiratory problems and eye issues, such as deformed tear ducts (this is also true of brachy cat breeds like the Persian). So brachycephalic breeds are more prone to weepy eye and conjunctivitis. In addition to the Holland lop, brachycephalic rabbit breeds include the Jersey wooly, Lionhead, and Netherland dwarf, while lop breeds include the English lop, French lop, Mini lop, and American fuzzy lop. Rabbits are pretty different anatomically from dogs, but one thing they have in common is that smaller breeds and mixed breeds tend to live longer than large or giant breeds and purebreds. Most importantly, before you decide to run out and get an adorable lop or brachy faced dwarf, remember that these breeds often experience more pain or discomfort in their day to day lives than plain old erect-eared, standard faced rabbits. Personally, I feel it's unethical to breed lops, or to breed for brachycephaly. It's done out of human vanity, with little or no thought as to the well-being of the animals who have to live with what are essentially deformities that we think are “cute".

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Should I separate both my rabbits until they're fixed? Will it be stressful to them? 1 male, 1 female, 4mths old frm the same litter. I wanted to get them fixed but the vet said to wait til abt 6mths old, and my male has started mounting the female.
Answer: Unless you want lots of kits, separate them immediately. Your female could potentially already be pregnant, although males reach sexual maturity somewhat earlier than females (around three to four months, as opposed to four to six months). Pregnancy is also stressful to does, and will be more stressful in one so young. (Having your brother constantly trying to mount you will also stress you out.) Also be advised that once they are adults and both have been spayed and neutered, they may not get along. Juvenile rabbits, both bucks and does, form “baby bonds" that can very well be broken once they reach adulthood, as a rabbit's behavior and personality can change from kittenhood to adulthood. A lot of people think that spaying or neutering changed their rabbit's personality, but often it's just that they're typically altered right around the time they're becoming adults, and their behavioral or personality differences are just due to growing up. But yes — separate them ASAP. And you may want to take your doe to the vet to make sure she isn't already pregnant.

Question: What are some of the most morally justified crimes ever committed?
Answer: The murder of Dee Dee Blancharde. 48-year-old Dee Dee Blancharde was found stabbed to death in her home in Springfield, Missouri, in June of 2015. Her disabled and terminally ill 19-year-old daughter, Gypsy Rose, was missing. Friends and neighbors feared the worst for Gypsy, who had developmental problems, leukemia, and muscular dystrophy, among other illnesses. Her wheelchairs were all still in the house, and Gypsy couldn't walk. Then Gypsy was found, safe and sound, in Wisconsin. She was also perfectly healthy — no leukemia, no muscular dystrophy, no developmental problems; nothing wrong with her at all. Gypsy and her boyfriend, Nicholas Godejohn, were arrested and charged with Dee Dee's murder. But if anyone was justified in committing such a crime, it was Gypsy. Dee Dee Blancharde, as it turned out, was a con artist and an abusive mother. Dee Dee had Factitious Disorder Imposed on Another, formerly known as Munchausen Syndrome By Proxy — a disorder that causes people to either feign or induce illness in a child or other loved one with the hope of gaining attention, sympathy, or financial rewards. From the time Gypsy was an infant, Dee Dee had been conjuring up various illnesses for her and subjecting her to medical treatments and surgeries that she did not need. She routinely shaved Gypsy's head, to mimic the effects of chemotherapy, and had her salivary glands removed, which led to Gypsy losing most of her teeth before she was even a teenager. She also convinced Gypsy that she was four years younger than she actually was. Whenever one of Gypsy's doctors became suspicious, Dee Dee found a new doctor. Gypsy's father, Rod Blanchard (Dee Dee added the “e" at the end of her surname for unknown reasons after her divorce) was seven years younger than Dee Dee, and only 17 when Gypsy was born; he and Dee Dee split shortly thereafter, and while Rod tried to stay in Gypsy's life, and faithfully paid child support each month, Dee Dee kept finding reasons to keep him away from his daughter. She moved Gypsy from Louisiana to Springfield, Missouri, where she told new friends and neighbors that Gypsy's father was a deadbeat, a lowlife drug addict who did nothing for his daughter — a bald-faced lie. Dee Dee also had everyone convinced that Gypsy was mentally disabled, and Gypsy was not allowed to spend time with anyone without Dee Dee present. She was trapped, and her only escape from her mother's domination of her was using the internet after Dee Dee fell asleep. (Dee Dee did catch her once; her response was to smash Gypsy's computer and chain her daughter to her bed.) When Gypsy met Godejohn online on a Christian dating site, the plans began to come together. In June of 2015, Godejohn, who was autistic and had an IQ of 82, traveled to Springfield. While Dee Dee was sleeping, Godejohn stabbed her 17 times while Gypsy waited outside, covering her ears so she did not have to hear her mother's screams. The couple then fled to Godejohn's native Wisconsin, which is where they were apprehended a few days later, and the truth came out that there was nothing physically wrong with Gypsy at all — everything had been fabricated by her mother. Gypsy herself learned that she was not actually 19, but 24. Although otherwise healthy, she was also significantly underweight, and subsequently gained almost 15 pounds in jail. Gypsy accepted a plea deal and was sentenced to 10 years in prison for second degree murder. Godejohn was convicted of first degree murder and sentenced to life without parole. Rod Blanchard and his wife Kristy have been supportive of Gypsy, who is now 31 and will be eligible for parole in December of this year. One thing Gypsy said in an interview will never leave me: I feel like I'm more free in prison, than living with my mom. Because now, I'm allowed to just live like a normal woman.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: How can someone be “priced out of their home” if they already own their home?
Answer: My friend Rita sold her house a few years ago, and bought another, smaller one in the same neighborhood. Her old house was a gorgeous, 19th century lakefront colonial, with a custom chef's kitchen (Rita does custom kitchens for a living), vaulted ceilings, stone fireplace, and a window wall overlooking the lake, and she owned it outright, having purchased it with her ex-husband over 30 years prior. It was property taxes that drove her out. Her property taxes were in excess of $33,000 a year, because she lived on prime real estate — there's only so much lakefront property on any given lake — in a fairly affluent town in the NYC metro area. In addition to that, local school taxes were $14,000 annually. That means that even without a mortgage, she was paying $4,000 a month just in taxes, and although she does well for herself, she is getting to an age where she's considering retirement, and that was just too much money. So as much as she loved her house, she sold (and she got a million dollars for it, which was less than her asking price, but still made her a nice profit). Her property taxes in the new house? $8,500 a year. Again, it's a smaller house, with no lakefront property, and on a smaller lot, but she still has lake rights, and especially with the profit she made from the sale of her old house, she also has a lot more financial room to breathe.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What actor/actress was nominated for a Best Supporting Oscar playing the title role in a movie?
Answer: Do you mean title role or main role? If the latter counts, Timothy Hutton was not only nominated, but won the Best Supporting Actor Oscar in 1981 for his film debut in Ordinary People. To this day he remains the youngest winner in the category, having been 20 at the time. But Hutton was quite clearly the lead — he appeared in almost every scene and had to carry a large portion of the film. However, it was, again, his first movie, and nobody knew who the hell he was. He was also billed fourth, behind his more established, famous costars Mary Tyler Moore, Donald Sutherland, and Judd Hirsch, and that's why I believe he was nominated in Supporting rather than lead. (Hirsch was also nominated in the same category.) I personally think Hutton should have been nominated as Best Actor, and his Supporting nomination should have gone to Sutherland, whom I feel was snubbed; he gave a terrific performance, and yet was the only main cast member not nominated (Moore was nominated for Best Actress). But frankly, if Hutton had been nominated in the lead category, he would almost surely not have won, because I don't think anyone was beating out Robert De Niro for Raging Bull that year. So being nominated in the wrong category probably worked out well for Hutton.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What billionaires were not born into wealth and privilege?
Answer: Oprah Winfrey. She was born in Kosciusko, Mississippi, to an unwed teenage mother, Vernita Lee, and for the first six years of her life, was raised by her maternal grandmother, Hattie. They were so poor that her grandmother made Oprah's dresses out of potato sacks. At six she moved to Milwaukee, Wisconsin with her mother, who worked as a maid, and also lived for a time with her father, Vernon Winfrey, a barber, in Nashville, Tennessee. She started high school in Milwaukee at Lincoln High School, but participated in the Upward Bound program, and excelled in academics, so was transferred to Nicolet High School, a more upscale school in the affluent suburb of Glendale. However, she was surrounded by wealthier children, and frustrated with her family's poverty, began stealing money from her mother in an attempt to “keep up with the Joneses”, leading her mother to send her back to Nashville to live with Vernon. Her father was much more strict than her mother, as well as more encouraging, and insisted that her education be top priority. She became an honors student, and was voted “most popular” in her senior class at East Nashville High School. She was also on the speech team, and won an oratory contest that earned her a full scholarship to Tennessee State University, where she studied communications. However, by the time she actually got her bachelor's degree, she was in her thirties and had already become a successful television personality. Love her or hate her, Oprah Winfrey started with absolutely nothing, and overcame tremendous odds to become the richest African-American of the 20th century, all by virtue of her own intelligence and hard work. Today her net worth is $2.5 billion.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: As a white person, when did you start to realize not all white people are your allies and not all black people your enemies?
Answer: I never realized it, because there was never a time in my life that I felt either that white people were my allies or black people were my enemies. I grew up in a small town 50 miles north of New York City that was overwhelmingly white and middle class. However, my parents, bless their souls, were two of the least racist people you could meet, and were both NYC natives. From the time I was very little we were a host family for kids in the Fresh Air Fund, a nonprofit in NYC that sends disadvantaged city kids to the Hudson Valley for a few weeks in summer to spend some time in the country. All of the kids who stayed with us were black, and we played with them like all our other friends. A couple of them even came back several years in a row. I was bullied all throughout school — mostly just for being “weird”, although I also changed schools often and had the misfortune of always being the “new kid”. From preschool up through 4th grade, all of the kids who bullied me were white kids. Every one of them. So I learned as early as preschool that not all white people were my allies. I had a few Asian classmates in kindergarten, but other than our Fresh Air Fund kids, I didn't really know any black people until I was in the 5th grade, when we moved to the Bronx after my parents' divorce. In the 5th grade, I had an experience I'll never forget, where I, the weird new kid, was being bullied and taunted in the schoolyard by a bunch of girls (of various races). The person who came to my rescue was Tanisha, another classmate — a very tall, skinny black girl with pretty braids, who put an arm around my shoulders and led me away from that group of jeering girls, talking calmly to me, and stayed with me until I calmed down. I had one other defender at PS 83, a Puerto Rican girl named Iris, who would leap in and verbally assault anyone she saw picking on me. Both Iris and Tanisha were well-liked and fairly popular, and I wasn't really friends with either outside of school; neither of them had to step up and defend me, but both of them did. And while there were a few black and brown girls among my bullies, I didn't see them any differently than the white girls who bullied me — the mean girls were the mean girls, and mean girls come in every shade. I never attributed their treatment of me to their race. Sometimes kids are little assholes, and that's universal. The idea that there are people who see other people as either allies or enemies based simply on skin color is just wild to me. Over the course of my life, I'd say about 95% of the people who have mistreated me have been fellow white people. Whether someone is a good or bad person has nothing to do with skin tone. People are individuals.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Which Breakfast Club relationship lasted longer: Andrew & Allison or Bender & Claire?
Answer: I'd put my money on Andy and Allison. Unlike John and Claire, they seemed to share an actual connection, one not based on socioeconomic status (John) or rebellion against their parents (Claire). Andy connected with Allison well before Claire gave her that makeover (which she didn't need anyway), and Allison — who was, I think, the most observant and true-to-self of the five leads — had a very good understanding of who Andy was from very early on. Honestly, I didn't really question it back then, but watching the film now, I can't for the life of me understand the John/Claire hookup. John treats Claire like absolute dogshit throughout the entire movie. He insults her, he sexually harasses her (actually sexually assaults her, if you remember), basically treats her as the personification of all his own troubles and insecurities. And Claire is easily my least favorite of the five main characters, she's bland as hell and I don't even like her much, but she didn't deserve that kind of treatment, and John certainly didn't deserve to be rewarded for his treatment of her. I get it, his parents were abusive, and that automatically makes him more sympathetic. But it still doesn't excuse his own abusive treatment of Claire. I'd give John and Claire a couple months, maybe. Andy and Allison could possibly go the distance. Fun fact: during the filming of the movie, it was Molly Ringwald (Claire) and Anthony Michael Hall (Brian) who dated each other; both are the same age and were well younger than the other three actors.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Do living writers ever choose to withdraw their past books from publication?
Answer: Stephen King did this with Rage, a novel he'd written in 1977 under his pen name Richard Bachman. The novel is about a Maine high school student named Charlie Decker, who brings a gun to school and fatally shoots two of his teachers, then holds his classmates hostage. Six different school shooters in the 1990s were at least partly inspired by the novel, so when it went out of print in the U.S., King opted not to renew it. He later took it out of print worldwide. In 2013, following the Sandy Hook shootings, King published a nonfiction e-book essay called Guns, detailing why he had taken the novel out of circulation, and donated all proceeds from the sale of the book to the Brady Campaign to Prevent Gun Violence.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: How did my rabbit get GI stasis when I always fed him grass and fruits?
Answer: Fruit is terrible for rabbits. Their digestive systems aren't designed to digest sugar. Too much sugar will give a rabbit a stomachache and upset their gut flora, and that will make them stop eating, leading to stasis. Fiber. Lots and lots of fiber, preferably from grass hay and chew toys made from safe woods like willow and apple. That, plus a daily serving of dark, leafy greens and herbs, is a proper rabbit diet. Fruit should only be given in very small quantities — half a strawberry, a few blueberries, a small slice of banana, etc. — a couple times a week as a treat. Like it or not, rabbits have very sensitive digestive systems, that can be thrown out of whack very easily if they're not fed the proper diet.

Question: Did Emilio Estevez play Mexican characters?
Answer: No, not a one. And why should he? He's not Mexican. He's not even Mexican-American. He is of English and Scottish ancestry on his mother's side, and Spanish and Irish ancestry on his father's side. Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What are the best Netflix original series?
Answer: This is subjective, obviously, but my favorite Netflix original series is hands down The Haunting of Hill House (2018). Here you have what is ostensibly a horror series, written, produced, and directed by one of today's most highly regarded horror filmmakers, Mike Flanagan, but what you get in the end is probably one of the best family dramas of the modern era. For the uninitiated, Hill House is a 10-episode series loosely based on Shirley Jackson's 1959 novel, which it tweaks and updates, with the past sequences set in 1992 and the current ones in the modern day (2018). It's about the Crain family — dad Hugh (Henry Thomas then, Timothy Hutton now), mom Olivia (Carla Gugino), and kids Steven (Paxton Singleton/Michiel Huisman), Shirley (Lulu Wilson/Elizabeth Reaser), Theodora AKA “Theo” (Mckenna Grace/Kate Siegel), and twins Luke (Julian Hilliard/Oliver Jackson-Cohen) and Nell (Violet McGraw/Victoria Pedretti). The family moves into the titular Hill House in 1992 intending to flip and sell it, but things go horribly awry. All of the adult Crain children are some level of emotionally and psychologically fucked up, stemming largely from their childhood experiences in the haunted mansion. Their mother died when they were kids, their relationships with one another are fractured, and none of them have anything even approaching a relationship with their father. Starting with the first episode, each Crain child gets his or her own focus episode, starting with Steve, the oldest, and ending with Nellie, the younger twin by less than two minutes. Hugh and Olivia each also get episodes focusing on them. Episode 6, which sees the mostly estranged family reunite for a funeral, is probably one of the best episodes I've ever seen of any show, both from a technical standpoint and an artistic one. It's almost an hour long, yet was filmed with only five shots, the longest of which was a full 17 minutes. And during these long shots, the actors had to deliver some heavy, emotional shit; I can only imagine the fear each must have had of screwing up their lines and ruining the shot. Flanagan called the episode “the hardest thing we've ever done, and the result of the combined efforts of hundreds of people”. The child actors, who ranged in age from 6 to 13, not only look a lot like the adults who play the grown up versions of them, all of them can actually act. I was probably most impressed with little Violet McGraw (who can currently be seen in theaters in the horror film M3GAN), who had some heavy shit to play as a 6-year-old, but all of them were excellent. So were the adults; if there was a weak link, it was Huisman, but given that he's Dutch and English is like his third language, he played American pretty damn convincingly. Pedretti, meanwhile, landed the role of Nell right out of college, and she was absolutely dynamite. Flanagan regulars Annabeth Gish and Robert Longstreet are also customarily excellent as the somewhat mysterious caretakers of Hill House, Horace and Clara Dudley, as are Anthony Ruivivar, Samantha Sloyan, and Levy Tran as the respective significant others of Shirley, Steve, and Theo. I am an unabashed Mike Flanagan fan, and love quite a lot of his work — Hush, Doctor Sleep, Gerald's Game, Midnight Mass, The Midnight Club — but for me, Hill House is his masterpiece. This isn't just a horror series — it's much more than that.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: How do you decide which pet to get for your kid?
Answer: First, immediately disqualify any pet whose care you're not willing to take responsibility for, which is basically every pet if the child is under age 10 or so. Kids under, say, five or six shouldn't have any pets — at that age, pets should be family pets. A five-year-old can help — they can feed the cat, the fish, the hamster, the budgie, etc. — but cleaning tanks and cages is going to be your job as the parent. It's just not something young kids can do properly. Other small pets, like guinea pigs, have more specialized diets, and a young kid can't be responsible for feeding them. (Guinea pigs, while delightful, are also messy little poop machines, so their cages need to be cleaned often.) And for the love of all that's good in the world, never get a rabbit for a child until the kid is at least 10 or 11. Rabbits are possibly the worst pets you can get for small children. They're complicated to care for, they're long-lived, and frankly, they generally don't like kids very much, because kids want to cuddle and carry them around, and rabbits almost universally hate both of those things. For young kids, a family pet like a dog or cat is probably best, although they still need supervision while interacting with them. Really the only small animal pet I recommend for kids aged 5–10 are rats, kept in same-sex pairs since they're social. Rats are intelligent and fairly sturdy, they rarely bite or nip, they can be very affectionate, they're relatively easy to care for, and with a lifespan of about 3 years, they're not a long-term commitment. Whatever pet you're thinking of getting your kid, don't do it before doing thorough research on the animal's behavior and proper care. In the internet age, there is no excuse not to know what you're getting into before taking on the responsibility of another creature's life.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: I am moving to Denver this summer with 2 dogs and 4 cats. Trying to find rentals with flexible pet policies has been tough. Does anyone know of any spots (I.e., apartments, houses, condos)?
Answer: I hate to break it to you, but Denver zoning laws prohibit having more than five dogs and cats combined per household. So within the city of Denver, it's not legal for you to have two dogs and four cats in one residence (and even if it were, most landlords are unlikely to allow that many, especially in an apartment). The city also requires by law that dogs and cats be spayed and neutered by the age of six months, unless you apply for a special permit, and pit bulls are banned in Denver without a permit, so hopefully your pets are all fixed and neither of your dogs are pitties. You may want to check the surrounding suburbs instead. Again, Denver only allows a certain number of pets per household based on species — I have a rabbit, and you can't have more than two of those in Denver legally. (EDIT: I just want to note that I am in no way knocking Denver. It's a great city, and if I were ever to live in a city again, it would be high on my list. But they do have heavy regulations when it comes to pets.)

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Are hamsters or guinea pigs better as small pets? Why?
Answer: They're totally different behaviorally, and require different care, so it depends what you want in a pet. Personally, my opinion is that if you want a pet that's more interactive, guinea pigs are the way to go. They're dear, sweet little creatures who usually become accustomed to handling pretty easily. But note that they're a longer term commitment than hamsters because of their longer lifespan, and I will stress again that they're very social and should not be kept alone, or they can become depressed. So always get at least two guinea pigs of the same sex. And also always remember that the vast majority of commerical cages sold at pet stores for both species are too small and thus inadequate. Proper cages can be found online.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Which movie villain would be considered a hero in a different film?
Answer: Little Bill Daggett in Unforgiven. In fact, I'd go so far as to say that Little Bill would be the hero in the same movie had the story been told from his perspective. The film is intentionally somewhat ambiguous as concerns its antagonist, Little Bill (Gene Hackman), and its protagonist, Will Munny (Clint Eastwood). It's all about whose perspective you're viewing the story from. Unforgiven tells the story from Will's perspective, so Will is the one we identify with. But the same story told from Little Bill's point of view would look different. SPOILERS AHEAD. It's 1881, and Little Bill is the sheriff of Big Whiskey, Wyoming. One night, two local ranch hands, Quick Mike and Davey Bunting, visit the town brothel, where a prostitute named Delilah (Anna Thomson) makes the mistake of laughing at Mike's diminutive penis, leading him to cut her face and disfigure her in a rage. Little Bill orders that the brothel owner, Skinny DuBois, be compensated for loss of revenue (due to Delilah now being seen as less desirable) with payment in horses, but the two men are not punished other than in the loss of the horses, although a contrite Davey — the one who did not cut her — offers her personally (as opposed to Skinny) his best horse as compensation. Outraged by the lack of punishment, the other prostitutes in the brothel, led by Strawberry Alice (Frances Fisher) secretly pool their money and offer a $1,000 bounty for the two men's deaths. Meanwhile, in Kansas, a cocky young man calling himself the Schofield Kid (Jaimz Wolvett) seeks out infamous outlaw and murderer Will Munny, who is now a widower raising his two kids on a hog farm, and tells him about the bounty, requesting his help. Will, in need of money, recruits his old pal Ned Logan (Morgan Freeman), and they head off to Big Whiskey. Also in pursuit of the bounty is English Bob (Richard Harris), a gunfighter and killer who has with him his own biographer to document his exaggerated tales. Because guns are illegal in Big Whiskey, Little Bill and his deputies disarm and then severely beat Bob and throw him in jail when he refuses to leave town. The Kid manages to kill Quick Mike, but the act overwhelms him with remorse, and he forsakes the mission. Will successfully kills Davey (who, we should remember, committed no actual crime) after Ned also realizes that he doesn't want to kill the man. But Ned is then captured by Little Bill, who tortures him to find out Will's true identity, and then kills him. The Kid, meanwhile, goes back to Kansas with the reward money, which he gives to Ned's wife and Will's kids. Will seeks out Little Bill to avenge Ned's death. He kills Skinny along with three of Bill's deputies before killing Bill himself, then leaves town after promising to come back if any more of the prostitutes are harmed. The epilogue suggests that Will took his kids to San Francisco and became a prosperous dry goods merchant. Now, really, what made Little Bill a villain? Sure, he didn't whip or imprison the man who cut Delilah, instead offering Skinny the only compensation, but if you consider the times, that's not terribly surprising. And that's literally the only thing he does that can really be considered “bad". We see him as savage for the beating of English Bob, but Bob was actually a way worse person than Bill, a murderer and a braggart, and he was breaking the law by trying to bring guns into town. We also hate him for what he does to Ned, because we love Ned, but really, Ned brought it on himself by seeking the bounty in the first place. So did Will — who, by the way, is a man who has killed women and children in his time, not some hero. And is death really a fair punishment for the two men anyway? Especially Davey, who never laid a hand on Delilah, and even tried to compensate her for the actions of his friend? Will is the hero and Little Bill is the villain only because the story is told from Will's point of view. We travel with Will and Ned, we get to know them, and so we sympathize with them, not with Little Bill, who's really just a lawman trying to maintain order in a Wild West town. Little Bill is tough, but he's also mostly fair. The movie even kind of acknowledges this, as right before Will kills him, Little Bill says “I don't deserve to die this way". And Will tells him, “’deserve’ ain't got nothing to do with it”. The ambiguity of the story is one of the things that makes Unforgiven such a great film, but the fact remains that the vast majority of people who watch the movie are going to see Little Bill as the villain — due almost entirely to perspective. EDIT: Comments are now disabled. For one, because there are people who can't agree to disagree and want to turn this into a debate site, which it is not, and for another, because the point of the answer is apparently flying over too many heads. I wrote the answer straight up — related the plot of the film mostly as it's given to us. And everyone is commenting based on the POV we're given in the film — Will's POV. When the answer literally says that if it was told from from Little Bill's perspective, he could well be the “hero". Instead of starting with Will on his hog farm, start with Little Bill trying to finish building his damn house, and follow the events of the film from his point of view. It looks different. I'm not debating this anymore. Anyone who thinks it's a bad answer is free to downvote it, because I honestly don't care anymore. Have at it.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: I'm living in an apartment. Is it a good idea to get a bunny/rabbit as pet?
Answer: That depends. As long as you do your research beforehand to make sure a rabbit is the right pet for you — rabbits are long-lived and fairly high-maintenance animals, and do not behave like dogs or cats — and have enough space for at least a 4′x4′ exercise pen, apartment life is fine for rabbits. Certainly it's much better than keeping them in hutches outdoors. I live in a 700 square foot apartment. My rabbit's pen is in my living room, and in the evenings he has free roam of the entire room. (I've recently given him the option of going into the bedroom, but he hates the hard floors and mostly stays on the rug or his blanket, although I suspect he will eventually get curious enough to venture in.) As long as you rabbit-proof by protecting baseboards, carpeting, electrical cords, etc., and litter train the rabbit — neither of which are very difficult — you'll be fine. I would actually suggest getting two rabbits if you're not home all the time, as rabbits are social and need company. Having said that, if you're thinking a rabbit might be a good option because you live in a small space and can keep it in a cage — meaning the sort of small cage generally advertised for rabbits — I would say don't do it. Rabbits don't belong in cages, and the aforementioned 4′x4′ ex pen is the smallest recommended enclosure for one rabbit. Question: Is there any example of an actor whose character dies in the first movie role of said actor?
Answer: Alan Rickman, in Die Hard. Rickman was a lauded stage actor, but he did not make his big screen debut until he was cast as baddie Hans Gruber in Die Hard at age 41. Hans famously falls to his death from the top of Nakatomi Plaza at the film's climax. Brad Dourif, in One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest. Dourif was 24 when he appeared as timid, stuttering Billy Bibbitt in Milos Forman's 1975 adaptation of Ken Kesey's novel. Billy, of course, commits suicide at the end of the movie when Nurse Ratched threatens to tell his domineering mother he slept with a prostitute. Lukas Haas, in Testament. Haas was just 6 when he played the youngest child of Jane Alexander and William Devane in this 1983 drama, set in the aftermath of nuclear war. His character, Scottie, dies from radiation poisoning. Mary Elizabeth Mastrantonio, in Scarface. Mastrantonio played Gina Montana, the younger sister of Al Pacino's Tony Montana. She gets gunned down at the end of the film. Question: Who is the greatest English speaking actor/actress to have never been nominated for an Academy Award?
Answer: As much as I love Donald Sutherland, the only real answer to this question is… … Alan Rickman. It doesn't seem possible, but somehow he never received a single Oscar nomination. Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: How can white/Caucasian people show their pride yet not seem racist?
Answer: White person here. The very idea of “white pride" is inane to me. “White" isn't a culture or ethnicity, so how is it something to be proud of? Take a lobsterman in Maine, a lawyer in New York City, an insurance salesman in Des Moines, a rancher in Texas, and a shop owner in Seattle. Say they're all white. What else do they have in common? Other than all being Americans, something Americans of every race and skin color have in common? What on earth are the lobsterman and the insurance salesman going to talk about? They're unlikely to like the same sports teams. Iowa is 1,200 miles from the nearest ocean. Okay, maybe they both love Bruce Springsteen, or are into horror movies, but that's nothing to do with being white, any more than liking the same sports teams is. Their ancestors are unlikely to even have come from the same place; the largest ethnicity in Iowa is German, in Maine it's English. The local culture is different in those two states, too; you're throwing a New England Damnyankee in with a Midwesterner. There are millions of white people in my country that I have absolutely nothing in common with other than a general lack of melanin in my skin. Stick me in some dusty town in Oklahoma, or the wilds of Alaska, and I'm going to be a fish out of water no matter how many white people I meet. I certainly can't see myself bonding with the locals over our shared whiteness. I am not proud of being white. I don't see it as anything to be proud of; my race has very little to do with who I am as a person, and I didn't ask to be white, nor is it something I somehow achieved — it just happened that way. (EDIT: I should clarify, I'm not ashamed to be white, either. I don't derive either pride or shame from it.) And that's another thing. I understand racial and ethnic pride in marginalized groups. That's how St. Patrick's Day and Columbus Day first became widely celebrated holidays among Irish-Americans and Italian-Americans, respectively — because both of those ethnic groups were at one time marginalized in U.S. society. My own father experienced that discrimination firsthand in the 1920s and 30s. Irish pride and Italian pride were those people asserting their right to celebrate their own culture despite others discriminating against them and trying to keep them down. Saying, “I'm Irish/Italian, and that's okay.” And that's what black pride and LGBTQ+ pride are today. But white pride? I don't know what that even means outside of the white supremacy movement. So, what's the pride you feel in being white? It's not an accomplishment. It's not a culture. It's a broad term for people of all or mostly European ancestry with fair skin. So I'm afraid I'm stuck at the whole “show their pride” thing, because I don't see anything inherent in simply being white to feel pride in.

Question: How much parsley can I feed my rabbit a day? Does the amount matter?
Answer: I would not feed parsley daily. Maybe a few times a week in moderation, or every other week. Parsley is high in oxalic acid (as are spinach and mustard greens), which is toxic in higher amounts, so while a small amount of parsley a few times a week is very healthy, with lots of vitamins and nutrients, you should be cautious in feeding too much or too often. I usually don't give my rabbit (or my guinea pig) more than a few sprigs of parsley at a time, and it's also not a bad idea to only feed it at intervals, e.g. if you feed parsley one week, skip it the next week. (EDIT: there are other herbs that are also very healthy and are safe to feed every day, such as cilantro/coriander, dill, and basil.) But yes, the amount matters. Parsley can even be toxic to humans in larger quantities, and rabbits are a lot smaller and a lot more delicate than we are.
